original_interpretation: Yield is the percentage of usable dies produced on a processed wafer.
evidence_found: "Yield refers to the percentage of usable die that are produced on a processed wafer." (Intel Tech 101, section 'Measuring Process Nodes with Yield and PPA')
notes: URL now redirects to intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/tech101/explaining-common-chip-terms.html. Definition from a company explainer; standard industry definition, 'fact' acceptable.

original_interpretation: Intel defines a process node as the recipe and list of ingredients used in fabrication.
evidence_found: "The recipe and list of ingredients used in semiconductor fabrication is called a process node. A node specifies the physical architecture of the components..." (Intel Tech 101, 'Process Nodes and PDKs')
notes: Claim correctly attributes the definition to Intel.

original_interpretation: Intel (Sep 2023) announced glass substrates to replace organic substrates, delivery 2H of decade, up to 10x interconnect density.
evidence_found: "evaluating the reliability of glass substrates as a replacement for organic substrates"; "on track to deliver complete glass substrate solutions to the market in the second half of this decade"; "a 10x increase in interconnect density is possible on glass substrates" (Intel release, Sep 18 2023)
notes: Source says '10x increase ... is possible', claim says 'up to 10x' - equivalent. Forward-looking plan from 2023 correctly typed reported_claim; as of 2026-10 whether delivery happened was not verified here (search results suggest no commercial product yet; not opened, not cited).

original_interpretation: Mark Bohr (Intel) said in 2013 he could not point to a single dimension equal to the node name.
evidence_found: "But I'm the first to admit that I can't point to the one dimension that's 32 nm or 22 nm or 14 nm. Some dimensions are smaller than the stated node name, and others are larger." (IEEE Spectrum, Rachel Courtland, 28 Oct 2013)
notes: Article dated 28 Oct 2013; Bohr identified as Intel senior fellow.

original_interpretation: TSMC N2 uses first-generation nanosheet transistors.
evidence_found: "N2 technology features industry-leading first-generation nanosheet transistor technology, with full-node strides in performance and power consumption" (TSMC 2nm page)
notes: Self-description; 'industry-leading' is marketing and not part of the claim.

original_interpretation: TSMC states N2 started volume production in 4Q25.
evidence_found: "TSMC's 2nm (N2) technology has started volume production in 4Q25 as planned." (TSMC 2nm page, accessed 2026-10-01)
notes: Company statement; correctly a reported_claim.

original_interpretation: TSMC A16 combines nanosheet transistors with backside power rail for better density/performance.
evidence_found: "TSMC A16™ technology integrates leading nanosheet transistors with innovative backside power rail solution, bringing greatly improved logic density and performance." (TSMC A16 page)
notes: Page now also lists A12 as 'the second generation of innovative backside power rail solution', so A16 is the first generation; not part of claim.

original_interpretation: CoWoS is 2.5D, integrates SoCs + HBM on interposer; CoWoS-S interposer up to 3.3x reticle (~2,700 mm2).
evidence_found: "CoWoS® advanced 2.5D packaging technology"; "By integrating multiple SoCs and high-bandwidth memory stacks"; "CoWoS®-S can accommodate an interposer up to 3.3X-reticle size (or ~2700mm2)." (TSMC CoWoS page)
notes: Figure, unit and population match.

original_interpretation: CoWoS-L at 3.5x reticle in volume production since 2024.
evidence_found: "TSMC's first CoWoS®-L at 3.5X-reticle size has been in volume production since 2024. ... CoWoS®-L continues scaling the interposer size" (TSMC CoWoS page)
notes: Source says 'first CoWoS-L at 3.5X'; 3.5X is the first generation, not the maximum, as TSMC says it continues scaling interposer size.

original_interpretation: SoIC is wafer-level 3D stacking, bond pitch from sub-10um, 3nm stacking in volume production 2025.
evidence_found: "TSMC-SoIC® is an innovative wafer-level 3D IC chip stacking platform."; "The bond pitch starts from the sub-10µm rule."; "its 3nm chip stacking technology successfully entered volume production in 2025." (TSMC SoIC page)
notes: All three parts found verbatim.

original_interpretation: TSMC eFoundry gives online access to pilot lot, yield, WAT and Q&R data.
evidence_found: "The Engineering Collaboration includes online access to pilot lots, wafer yields, wafer acceptance test (WAT) analysis, and quality reliability data" (TSMC eFoundry page)
notes: Exact match.

original_interpretation: TSMC portal gives wafer lot status (fab, assembly/test, final test, order, shipping) updated 3x/day.
evidence_found: "The Logistics Collaboration provides access to data updated three times a day on a wafer lot's status in fabrication, assembly and testing, final testing, order, and shipping" (TSMC eFoundry page)
notes: SRC-0171 (pr.tsmc.com/english/news/2287, 2000-12-04) opened but extracted text was truncated and the 'three times daily' sentence was not visible; EE Times' 2000-12-04 report of the same release says customers can see "order and shipping status that is updated three times daily". Current page is the primary support.

original_interpretation: TSMC-Online for design info, tape-outs, wafer tracking; TSMC-Direct system-to-system integration.
evidence_found: "TSMC-Online is the first foundry delivery system to provide secure online business transactions and information transfer for product design, tape-outs, and wafer tracking."; "TSMC-Direct is a premium system-to-system integration service between TSMC and its business partners through third-party software." (TSMC eFoundry page)
notes: 'first foundry delivery system' is a self-claim not included in the claim.

original_interpretation: TSMC OIP has EDA certification program, largest silicon-verified IP catalog, and IP/EDA/DCA/Cloud/VCA/3DFabric alliances.
evidence_found: OIP page: "The foundry segment's earliest and most comprehensive electronic design automation (EDA) certification program"; IP tile: "the semiconductor industry's largest catalog of ecosystem-partner, silicon-verified,...". TSMC release 27 Oct 2022: "the TSMC OIP consists of six alliances: the EDA Alliance, IP Alliance, Design Center Alliance (DCA), Value Chain Alliance (VCA), Cloud Alliance, and now, the 3DFabric Alliance."
notes: OIP page text as extracted showed IP, EDA and Cloud alliance tiles only; full list of six confirmed in TSMC's 2022 release. 'Earliest', 'most comprehensive', 'largest' are TSMC self-descriptions (reported_claim correct).

original_interpretation: Samsung announced 30 Jun 2022 initial production of 3nm with GAA, calling MBCFET the first-ever GAA implementation.
evidence_found: "today announced that it has started initial production of its 3-nanometer (nm) process node applying Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistor architecture"; "Multi-Bridge-Channel FET (MBCFET™), Samsung's GAA technology implemented for the first time ever, defies the performance limitations of FinFET" (Samsung US Newsroom, 6/30/2022)
notes: SRC-0173 (global newsroom) did not render (web_extract returned only search UI; browser navigation timed out). Verified on Samsung's own US-newsroom copy of the same release, dated 6/30/2022 (Business Wire copy carries 2022-06-29 US time). 'First time ever' is Samsung's self-claim; reported_claim is correct.

original_interpretation: Samsung: 1st-gen 3nm GAA cuts power up to 45% vs 5nm.
evidence_found: "Compared to 5nm process, the first-generation 3nm process can reduce power consumption by up to 45%, improve performance by 23% and reduce area by 16% compared to 5nm" (Samsung US Newsroom, 6/30/2022, 'Design-Technology Optimization for Maximized PPA')
notes: Global newsroom copy unavailable to tools; same release on Samsung US newsroom. Manufacturer claim, test conditions not disclosed (metric methodology correct).

original_interpretation: JEDEC HBM4 (JESD270-4, 16 Apr 2025): up to 2 TB/s, 8 Gb/s, 2048-bit.
evidence_found: "With transfer speeds up to 8 Gb/s across a 2048-bit interface, HBM4 boosts total bandwidth up to 2 TB/s." (JEDEC release via Business Wire, Arlington VA, April 16 2025, 'Increased Bandwidth')
notes: jedec.org page blocked by Cloudflare in browser and web_extract returned only the title; verified on the verbatim Business Wire copy of the same release. 2048 bits x 8 Gb/s = 16.4 Tb/s = ~2 TB/s, consistent with the metric being per stack. Standard-specification maxima, not shipping-product speeds.

original_interpretation: HBM4 supports 4- to 16-high stacks of 24/32 Gb dies, up to 64 GB per stack.
evidence_found: "HBM4 supports 4-high, 8-high, 12-high and 16-high DRAM stack configurations with 24 Gb or 32 Gb die densities, providing for a higher cube density of 64GB (32 Gb 16-High)." (JEDEC release, 'Capacity' bullet, Design & Reuse republication)
notes: jedec.org original blocked for automated readers; checked against republished full text of the same release. 32 Gb x 16 = 512 Gb = 64 GB, arithmetic consistent.

original_interpretation: UCIe is a consortium die-to-die interconnect standard for an open chiplet ecosystem; current spec 3.0.
evidence_found: Home page: "Building an open ecosystem of chiplets for on-package innovations"; "The UCIe 3.0 Specification is here – setting the next stage for the evolution of open chiplet standards!" About page: "an open specification that defines the interconnect between chiplets within a package"
notes: Checked 2026-10-01; web search found no released UCIe 4.0 (only mention of a 4.0 proposal). Home page also shows a stale 'COMING SOON UCIe Specification 1.0' tile; ignore. 'Current = 3.0' is time-sensitive; recheck later.

original_interpretation: HBM stacks multiple DRAM dies connected with TSVs.
evidence_found: "A premium, high-performance technology which has revolutionized data processing speeds by vertically stacking multiple DRAMs using through-silicon via (TSV) ... it is none other than High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)." (SK hynix newsroom, May 2 2023)
notes: Company explainer; the description matches the JEDEC standard's stacked-die architecture (CLM-0441), so claim_type fact is acceptable.

original_interpretation: SK hynix began mass production of 321-layer 1Tb TLC NAND in Nov 2024, industry first.
evidence_found: "announced today that it has started mass production of the world's first triple level cell-based 321-high 4D NAND Flash with 1Tb capacity."; "The company plans to provide the 321-high products to customers from the first half of next year." (SK hynix, Seoul, November 21 2024)
notes: SK hynix calls it '4D NAND' (its brand for 3D NAND with periphery under cell); claim's '3D NAND' is fine. Customer shipments were planned from 1H 2025. 'World's first' is SK hynix's own claim.

original_interpretation: SKY130 PDK is a Google-SkyWater open-source collaboration under Apache 2.0, usable for manufacturable designs at SkyWater.
evidence_found: "The SkyWater Open Source PDK is a collaboration between Google and SkyWater Technology Foundry to provide a fully open source Process Design Kit ... which can be used to create manufacturable designs at SkyWater's facility."; "released under the Apache 2.0 license"; "Google and SkyWater are currently treating the current content as an experimental preview / alpha release." (README)
notes: All stated facts confirmed, but the claim leaves out the README warning that the release is an alpha / experimental preview.
correction: Add caveat: the README calls the open-source PDK an 'experimental preview / alpha release' that 'is not intended to be used for production settings at this current time' (usable for test chips).

original_interpretation: SKY130 PDK contains design-rule docs, EDA support files, analog primitive cells/models, standard digital cell libraries.
evidence_found: "Comprehensive documentation around the design rules required to create manufacturable devices on the SKY130 Process Node." "EDA tooling support files for multiple open source and proprietary design flows." "Primitive cell libraries and models for creating analog designs." "Multiple standard digital cell libraries" (README, 'PDK Contents')
notes: Exact match.

original_interpretation: Traditional RTL-to-GDSII flow is divided into synthesis, place-and-route, signoff.
evidence_found: "The traditional RTL-to-GDSII design flow has clear lines of demarcation between synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff functions." (Synopsys press release, 19 Mar 2018)
notes: The quote is there, but it is a vendor marketing release (pitching Fusion as removing these boundaries), so claim_type should be reported_claim, not fact. The same release names other flow steps (extraction, physical verification, DFT/ATPG, equivalence checking).
correction: Synopsys (2018 marketing release) describes the traditional flow as having demarcation between synthesis, place-and-route and signoff functions; this is a simplified three-way split, not a complete list of flow stages.

original_interpretation: SEMI P39 (OASIS) defines hierarchical mask-layout interchange format and succeeded GDSII Stream (de facto >20 years).
evidence_found: "The purpose of this Specification is to define an interchange and encapsulation format for hierarchical integrated circuit mask layout information."; "a working group to define a successor to the venerable GDSII Stream format, which had served the I.C. industry as a de facto standard for layout interchange for more than two decades." (SEMI P39 abstract)
notes: The source says OASIS was chartered as a successor (from 2001). It does not say OASIS actually replaced GDSII in practice.
correction: OASIS was designed as the successor to GDSII Stream; the source does not establish that it displaced GDSII (say 'was created to succeed', not 'succeeded').

original_interpretation: GDSII's 16/32-bit fields and inefficient geometry led to files of many tens of GB; OASIS aimed for >=10x smaller files.
evidence_found: "The old format, limited by 16-bit and 32-bit internal integer fields, by its inefficient representation of cell-native geometric figures, and by high structural overhead, was becoming difficult to use ... file sizes were becoming unwieldy, in some cases growing to many tens of gigabytes."; "Achieve at least an order-of-magnitude file size improvement compared to GDSII Stream."
notes: Source says 'in some cases'. It lists the integer-width limit next to file size but does not say the integer fields caused the large files; the matching goal was 64-bit capability.
correction: Files reached many tens of GB only 'in some cases'; the source does not say the 16/32-bit integer limits caused the file sizes (they set a separate goal: full 64-bit capability).

original_interpretation: SEMI E142 defines data items for substrate map data (wafer, frame, strip, tray), supporting wafer-to-final-test tracking.
evidence_found: "SEMI E142, Specification for Substrate Mapping, defines data items that are required to report, store, and transmit map data for substrates such as wafers, frames, strips, and trays."; "alignment of XY coordinates is critical for single device tracking from the wafer through assembly to final test." (SEMI Standards Watch, Apr 16 2026)
notes: Article also says a major revision (Doc 7381, coordinate-mapping subordinate standard) was to be balloted Aug 19-Sep 18 2026 and adjudicated at SEMICON West in October 2026; the claim may need updating after that.

original_interpretation: SEMI E30 (GEM) defines standard SECS-II implementation for all equipment, governing equipment-host communication.
evidence_found: "1.1 GEM defines a standard implementation of SECS-II for all semiconductor manufacturing equipment."; "2.1 The scope of the GEM Standard is limited to defining the behavior of semiconductor equipment as viewed through a communications link. The SEMI E5 (SECS-II) Standard provides the definition of messages ... exchanged between host and equipment." (SEMI E30 abstract)
notes: Latest listed revision is SEMI E30-0526 (May 2026).

original_interpretation: Photomasks are high-precision quartz or glass plates with microscopic circuit images.
evidence_found: "photomasks, which are high precision photographic quartz or glass plates containing microscopic images of electronic circuits" (Photronics Form 10-K, fiscal year ended October 31 2025, Item 1 Business)
notes: Opened on SEC EDGAR; FY ended 2025-10-31, the latest 10-K.

original_interpretation: Photomasks sold in sets, each layer a distinct pattern on a different mask.
evidence_found: "Photomasks are typically sold in sets comprised of layers, with each layer having a distinct pattern that is etched onto a different photomask." (Photronics 10-K FY2025, Item 1)
notes: Exact match.

original_interpretation: Mask making starts with converting customer design data to pattern data, written by e-beam or laser lithography.
evidence_found: "The typical manufacturing process for a photomask involves the receipt and conversion of circuit design data to manufacturing pattern data. A lithography system then exposes the circuit pattern onto a photomask blank."; "manufacturing photomasks using electron beam or optical (laser-based) lithography systems" (Photronics 10-K FY2025, Item 1)
notes: Two passages from the same Item 1 combined correctly. The 10-K adds that FPD masks use only optical writers.

original_interpretation: Photronics: first layers sometimes needed within 24 hours of design data.
evidence_found: "The first several layers of photomasks are sometimes required to be delivered to customers within twenty-four hours from the time we receive customer design data." (Photronics 10-K FY2025, Item 1)
notes: Same paragraph: order-to-ship typically one day to three weeks.
